coredata.dc:description: A gene encoding poly(tetramethylene succinate), PBS, depolymerase, pbsA, has been cloned from Acidovorax delafieldii strain BS-3 chromosomal DNA. The clone expressed in Escherichia coli showed the ability to degrade both PBS and poly{(tetramethylene succinate)-co-adipate} that are kinds of biodegradable plastics. PBS depolymerase was considered to be a kind of lipase, since it also degrades olive oil. It had no apparent hydrophobic-amino-acid-rich region which exists in other known plastic-degrading enzymes. From the result of amino acid homology search, PbsA was found to have some similarities with lipases of Streptomyces sp. and Mollaxella sp. In the motif surrounding the active site Ser residue (Gly-X1-Ser-X2-Gly), PbsA was revealed to have a Trp residue in the X1 position instead of His which is most likely found in other bacterial lipases.

Institute of Applied Biochemistr), Universi~ of Tsukuba, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8572, Japan~ Received 27 August 2001/Accepted 5 November 2001 A gene encoding poly(tetramethylene succinate), PBS, depolymerase, pbsA, has been cloned from Acidovorax delafieldii strain BS-3 chromosomal DNA. The clone expressed in Escherichia coli showed the ability to degrade both PBS and poly{(tetramethylene succinate)-co-adipate} that are kinds of biodegradable plastics. PBS depolymerase was considered to be a kind of lipase, since it also degrades olive oil. It had no apparent hydrophobic-amino-acid-rich region which exists in other known plastic-degrading enzymes. From the result of amino acid homology search, PbsA was found to have some similarities with lipases ofStreptomyces sp. and Mollaxella sp. In the motif surrounding the active site Ser residue (Gly-X1-Ser-X2-Gly), PbsA was revealed to have a Trp residue in the X1 position instead of His which is most likely found in other bacterial lipases. [Key words: poly(tetramethylene succinate), depolymerase, Acidovorax] Poly(tetramethylene succinate), PBS, and poly{(tetrame- thylene succinate)-co-adipate}, PBSA, are synthetic polyes- ter-based polymers which have been developed as biode- gradable plastics. Although several PBS(A) degrading mi- crobes have been reported (1-7), there is only limited infor- mation about the key enzymes involved in PBS(A) biodeg- radation. Moreover, there is no information about the genes encoding PBS(A)-degrading enzymes. Previously, we reported Acidovorax delafieldii strain BS- 3 which uses PBS as the sole carbon and energy source (5). Strain BS-3 could use emulsified PBS, and both solid and emulsified PBSA. In this report, we present results of the molecular cloning and sequence analysis of the PBS de- polymerase gene (pbsA) from A. delafieldii strain BS-3 and its functional expression in Escherichia coli. The molecular distinctive characteristics of PbsA from other solid-poly- mer-degrading enzymes and lipases based on putative amino acid sequences are also discussed. PBS (Bionolle #1020) and PBSA (Bionolle #3020) used in this study were supplied by Showa Highpolymer Co. Ltd. (Tokyo). The number average molecular weights of PBS and PBSA are approximately 60,000. All other reagents were commercially available products. Unless specified otherwise, standard methods for DNA manipulation described by Maniatis et al. were followed (8). The total DNA extracted from strain BS-3 was partially digested with Sau3A I and fragments whose size ranged from 2 to 4 kbp were recovered using the QIAEX II agarose gel extraction kit (Qiagen, Germany). These fragments were then ligated to pUC 18 (9), which was digested with BamHI and dephosphorized, using a DNA ligation kit (Ligation High, Toyobo Co. Ltd., Tokyo) under conditions recom- * Corresponding author, e-mail: toshi@sakura.cc.tsukuba.ac.jp phone: +81-(0)298-53-4927 fax: +81-(0)298-53-4605 mended by the supplier. These recombinants were intro- duced into E. coli strain JM 109. For screening of the recombinant E. coli that exhibits PBS depolymerase activity, indicator plates were prepared as follows. The emulsified PBS (0.8%) solution containing 1.5% agar was prepared as described previously (5) and was overlaid on a Luria-Bertani (LB) agar plate (8). Among 16,800 recombinants, only one colony forming a clear-zone on the indicator plate was isolated. This clone could grow at both 30 and 37 C, but the clear-zone formation was ob- served only at 30 C. In addition, it took 2 or 3 d for clear- zone formation to be obtained. From this clone, the plasmid containing an approximately 4-kbp fragment derived from strain BS-3 was extracted and named pBSI. To determine the location of the gene on the 4-kbp fragment, the fragment was digested using several re- striction enzymes. The fragments obtained were subcloned into the appropriate sites in the pUCI 8 (or pUCI9) vector. The subcloning procedure is summarized in Fig. 1. The plasmids' ability to produce PBS depolymerase was investi- gated using the indicator plates. The gene responsible for clear-zone formation was located in pBS-ss7 which carried an approximately 1-kpb SacI-Smal fragment. In addition, transformants expressing PBS depolymerase could also de- grade PBSA and olive oil in addition to PBS (Fig. 1). This result strongly suggests that PBS depolymerase is a kind of lipase. The nucleotide sequence of the 1-kbp DNA fragment in- serted in pBS-ss7 was determined. The DNA fragment was sequenced by the dideoxy chain termination method de- scribed by Sanger et al. (10) using the ABI PRISM Big Dye Terminator Cycle Sequencing Core kit (Applied Biosys- terns, USA). The complete nucleotide sequence of the sense strand and its deduced amino acid sequence are shown in Fig. 2. The nucleotide sequence reported in this paper was 245 246 UCHIDA ET AL. J. The other plasmids were constructed using the pUCI9 vector. Each plasmid was introduced into E, coli strain JM109 and the strain was grown on various indicator plates for 3 d at 30 C. The computer analysis of the nucleotide sequence using the GENETYX-MAC program, version 8.0 (Software De- velopment Co. Ltd., Tokyo), detected one open reading frame (ORF), located between 1 and 912. The ORF consists of 912 bp with a putative GTG initiation codon, which is 8 bp downstream from a potential ribosome-binding site (-,3GGGCGA 8), and TGA as the stop codon. A potential promoter sequence similar to -10 and -35 consensus sequences of E. coli was found upstream of the ORF ( 55ACGAAT 50 and 83TTAGCA 78, respectively). The entire ORF molar G+C content was 66.6%. At the third position of the codon, G or C was found in 92.2% of the cases. It was concluded that this ORF codes for the PBS depolymerase gene named pbsA. The ORF encoded 304 amino acid resi- dues, capable of forming a 32,722-Da precursor protein. The first 41 deduced amino acids exhibited the characteris- tics of signal peptides with positively charged amino acids that are followed by hydrophobic amino acids. The nucleotide and amino acid sequences were computer- analyzed using FASTA (ver. 3.0) and BLAST (ver. 2.0) pro- grams (Table 1). From computerized search of databases, it was shown that PbsA had no homology with other known plastic-degrading esterases such as polyurethane esterase (PudA) (ll) and poly(hydroxyalkanoate) depolymerase (PhaZ) (12). PbsA showed very low homology with lipases derived from Pseudomonas spp., bacteria which are taxo- nomically similar to members of the genus Acidovorax. On the other hand, PbsA showed relatively high homol- ogy with lipases from Moraxella and Streptomyces that be- long to the family Neisseriaceae and actinomycetes, respec- tively (Table 1). It was reported that most of the known PBS-degrading bacteria belong to actinomycetes (1-4, 7). The relationship between actinomyces-type lipases and PBS degradation is still unknown because no PBS-degrading en- zyme genes from actinomycetes have been cloned. It is well known that most lipases and esterases contain a GIy-X1-Ser-X2-GIy motif, called lipase box, in their poly- peptide chain. The homologous region (~72Gly-Trp-Ser-Met- Gly176) was also found in PbsA. It is known that His is found in this position in a number of lipases from bacteria (13). This observation is only true in the lipase derived from Moraxella sp. strain TA144, a psy- chrophile strain isolated from Antarctic seawater (14). Unlike other water-soluble substrates, solid substrates are thought to have extremely low-contact efficiency with en- zyme molecules. Enzymes that degrade solid substrates are considered to have some functions that enable them to ad- sorb onto the surface of solid substrates. Plastic degradation by these enzymes is carried out in two steps, hydrophobic adsorption onto a plastic surface and degradation. In the previous report, we also demonstrated that PBS de- polymerase of strain BS-3 also degrades solid PBSA in two steps (5). However, although 48.4% of the amino acid resi- dues of PbsA were found to be hydrophobic, there was no apparent hydrophobic-amino-acid-rich region in PbsA. From this observation, PbsA was considered a novel plastic- degrading enzyme without a apparent hydrophobic-amino- acid-rich region. Further studies on the three-dimensional structure of PbsA are necessary. Although there have been several reports about PBS-de- grading bacteria (1-7) and their PBS-degrading enzymes, no information about their genes has been reported. In this study, we cloned a PBS depolymerase gene, pbsA, derived from A. delafieldii strain BS-3, and expressed it in E. coli. To our knowledge, this is the first report about a PBS de- polymerase gene from PBS-utilizing microorganisms. How- ever, further study is necessary to determine whether this gene is the only PBS depolymerase gene of strain BS-3. It may be possible that microbial PBS-degrading en- zymes will be classified as a new group in the lipase family if other genes of PBS-degrading enzymes from various mi- croorganisms are cloned and analyzed.
